sources: UNESCO World Heritage Centre — Historic Areas of Istanbul
meaningOfNames: Greek for 'Holy Wisdom', dedicated to the Wisdom of God rather than to a saint named Sophia.
longFormInfo: The domed cathedral of Constantinople built under Justinian I, later a mosque, a museum and again a mosque.
Construction began weeks after the Nika riots destroyed the previous church on the site.
Dedicated by Justinian I on 27 December 537. The first dome collapsed in 558 and was rebuilt higher by Isidore the Younger, rededicated in 562.

purpose: Built as the cathedral of Constantinople and seat of its patriarch. After the Ottoman conquest in 1453 it became a mosque; it was a museum from 1935 and a mosque again from 2020.
architecturalStyle: Byzantine: a domed basilica, its dome carried on pendentives
heritageStatus: UNESCO World Heritage Site (1985, as part of the Historic Areas of Istanbul)
significance: The largest building of the Byzantine world, whose dome set the model for Byzantine and later Ottoman architecture.
shortSummary: The sixth-century domed cathedral of Constantinople built for Justinian I in 532–537, converted to a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1935 and a mosque again in 2020.
longSummary: Justinian I rebuilt the church after the Nika riots of 532, with the mathematicians Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus as architects.
For nearly a thousand years it was the largest cathedral in the world and the setting of Byzantine imperial ceremony; crusaders sacked it in 1204.
Mehmed II made it a mosque after 1453, adding a minaret; later sultans added three more, and Mimar Sinan strengthened it with buttresses in the sixteenth century.
Atatürk's republic made it a museum, and it was reconverted to a mosque in 2020.
